output.problem: Frequent typhoons, earthquakes and volcanic eruptions cause significant losses and damage to government-owned public infrastructure. The explanatory note states that existing disaster policy under RA No. 10121 lacks a multi-layered, pre-arranged financial protection system for state-owned physical assets. The bill seeks a coordinated insurance and non-insurance financing strategy so that public assets can be repaired and rebuilt quickly and services can continue.
output.problem_quote: a significant structural gap remains: the absence of a multi-layered, pre-arranged financial protection system for state-owned physical assets.

rows.target_quote: This Act shall apply to all public infrastructure assets owned by the Government, including those owned under Republic Act No. 6957 or the Build-Operate-Transfer Law, as amended.

comparator.quote: Nothing in this Act shall require the Government to assume, insure, or finance a risk lawfully allocated to a private party under Republic Act No. 11966
comparator.title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK FINANCING AND INSURANCE FRAMEWORK, STRENGTHENING THE FINANCIAL PROTECTION OF PUBLIC ASSETS, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND VULNERABLE SECTORS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES

rows.differences: HB No. 10763 requires public-private partnership agreements on critical public assets to allocate disaster risks, insurance duties and retained risks, and states that the Government need not insure or finance risks lawfully allocated to a private party; this bill extends coverage to Build-Operate-Transfer assets without such a safeguard.
rows.why: Covering Build-Operate-Transfer assets without a risk-allocation safeguard could shift to the Government disaster risks that contracts already assign to private proponents.
rows.tradeoffs: The safeguard protects public funds but requires contract review to determine which risks each party bears.
rows.gap: Which covered assets are under contracts that already assign insurance obligations to private parties could not be established from the material.

rows.section_ref: Section 5 (Disaster Risk Financing and Insurance Council)
rows.target_quote: headed by the Secretary of the Department of Finance (DOF) as the Chairperson, and with the Secretary of the Department of Budget and Management (DBM)

comparator.quote: The Department of Finance (DOF), through the Bureau of the Treasury (BTr), in coordination with the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC), shall formulate
comparator.title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK FINANCING AND INSURANCE FRAMEWORK, STRENGTHENING THE FINANCIAL PROTECTION OF PUBLIC ASSETS, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND VULNERABLE SECTORS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES

rows.differences: HB No. 10763 assigns the disaster risk financing framework to the DOF through the BTr, in coordination with the NDRRMC and without prejudice to the NDRRMC's functions under RA No. 10121, instead of creating a new ten-agency council.
rows.why: Lodging the framework with the DOF and BTr, with formal coordination with the DBM, DEPDev, GSIS and NDRRMC, achieves the same purpose without adding a new inter-agency body alongside the NDRRMC.
rows.tradeoffs: Fewer bodies reduce coordination cost, but a single lead agency may secure less buy-in from the other members named in Section 5.
rows.gap: Whether existing coordination bodies already cover disaster risk financing for public assets, for purposes of RA No. 12231 streamlining, must be checked.

rows.section_ref: Section 6 (Powers and Functions of the DRFIC)
rows.target_quote: Manage and ensure the insurance of Government public assets

comparator.quote: The Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) shall continue to administer the insurance of government properties, assets, and insurable interests in accordance with Republic Act No. 656, as amended
comparator.title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK FINANCING AND INSURANCE FRAMEWORK, STRENGTHENING THE FINANCIAL PROTECTION OF PUBLIC ASSETS, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND VULNERABLE SECTORS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES

rows.differences: HB No. 10763 keeps the administration of government property insurance with the GSIS under RA No. 656 and leaves the asset registry with the BTr, whereas this bill gives the council itself the management of public asset insurance and the data integrity of the NARS.
rows.why: Giving the council operational insurance management and registry functions may duplicate the GSIS mandate under RA No. 656, as amended by PD No. 245, and the BTr's administration of the NARS; the council's role may be confined to policy, standards and monitoring.
rows.tradeoffs: A policy-only role avoids overlap but leaves operational accountability with the GSIS and BTr rather than one body.
rows.gap: The full list of council functions could not be reviewed because the section text is truncated after item (j).

comparator.quote: The GSIS may obtain reinsurance and other lawful risk-transfer protection from qualified domestic and foreign counterparties in accordance with Republic Act No. 656, as amended
comparator.title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK FINANCING AND INSURANCE FRAMEWORK, STRENGTHENING THE FINANCIAL PROTECTION OF PUBLIC ASSETS, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND VULNERABLE SECTORS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES

rows.differences: HB No. 10763 has the GSIS strengthen public asset protection through portfolio insurance, reinsurance and risk pooling with qualified counterparties, rather than a statutory consortium of all insurers and reinsurers offering public asset insurance.
rows.why: Reinsurance and risk pooling under the GSIS achieve collective risk sharing within the existing RA No. 656 framework without a new statutory consortium whose membership and governance are not defined.
rows.tradeoffs: Working through GSIS reinsurance avoids a new structure but may draw less private capacity than a consortium that all insurers join.
rows.gap: How membership in the consortium would be determined or made compulsory is not stated in the bill.

rows.differences: HB No. 10763 sets claims standards such as a definitive list of documents, provisional payment of undisputed amounts, written reasons for denial and a review mechanism, while this bill only requires the consortium to approve claims in a timely manner and to submit claims data to itself.
rows.why: Specific, time-bound claims standards give agencies an enforceable basis for prompt payment; the item requiring the consortium to submit data to itself may be corrected to name the receiving body.
rows.tradeoffs: Detailed standards speed payouts but limit insurers' discretion and may affect premium pricing.
rows.gap: The intended recipient of claims data under item (e) could not be established from the material.

rows.differences: HB No. 10763 keeps the NDRRMF under RA No. 10121 as part of risk retention and requires insurance recoveries to supplement it, whereas this bill carves out a separate DBM-managed fund whose releases also need council approval.

rows.tradeoffs: One fund simplifies management, but infrastructure needs may compete with relief needs within the NDRRMF.
rows.gap: The share of the current NDRRMF used for infrastructure repair and rehabilitation could not be established from the material.

memo_part.heading: On the Coverage of Public-Private Partnership Assets
paragraphs: 4.1 Section 4 (Coverage and Scope) of the bill extends coverage to public infrastructure assets owned under the Build-Operate-Transfer Law. It may be noted that some of these assets may be under contracts that already allocate disaster risks and insurance obligations to private proponents. In this regard, may we recommend that a safeguard be added, similar to Section 13 of HB No. 10763, providing that the Government shall not be required to assume, insure or finance risks lawfully allocated to a private party, to avoid shifting contractual risks to public funds.

memo_part.heading: On the Disaster Risk Financing and Insurance Council
paragraphs: 4.2 Section 5 (Disaster Risk Financing and Insurance Council) creates a new council chaired by the DOF with ten member agencies. It may be noted that an alternative arrangement, as in Section 4 of HB No. 10763, assigns the formulation of the disaster risk financing framework to the DOF through the BTr, in coordination with the NDRRMC and without prejudice to its functions under RA No. 10121. Consistent with the streamlining thrust of RA No. 12231, may we recommend that the framework be lodged with the DOF and BTr, with formal coordination with the DBM, DEPDev, GSIS and NDRRMC, in lieu of creating a new council.

4.3 Section 6 (Powers and Functions of the DRFIC) grants the council operational functions, including managing and ensuring the insurance of government public assets and ensuring the data integrity of the NARS. It may be noted that the insurance of government property is administered by the GSIS under RA No. 656, as amended by PD No. 245, and the NARS is administered by the BTr. In this regard, may we recommend that these operational functions be deleted and the council's or lead agency's role be confined to policy, standards, and monitoring and evaluation, to avoid duplication of functions.

memo_part.heading: On the National Public Asset Insurance Consortium
paragraphs: 4.4 Section 7 (National Public Asset Insurance Consortium) establishes a consortium of all insurance and reinsurance companies offering public asset insurance, led by the GSIS. It may be noted that the bill does not define how membership, governance and risk shares would be determined. May we recommend that the provision be revisited so that collective risk sharing is pursued through GSIS reinsurance and risk pooling with qualified domestic and foreign counterparties under RA No. 656, as amended, similar to Section 7 of HB No. 10763.

4.5 Section 8 (Functions of the NPAIC) requires the consortium to evaluate and approve government claims in a timely manner, and item (e) requires it to submit claims data to itself. May we recommend that simplified, transparent and time-bound claims standards be provided instead, including a definitive list of documentary requirements, provisional payment of undisputed amounts and written reasons for denial, similar to Section 11 of HB No. 10763, and that item (e) be corrected to name the body receiving claims data.

memo_part.heading: On the National Disaster Response for Infrastructure Fund and its Funding
paragraphs: 4.6 Section 9 (National Disaster Response for Infrastructure Fund) transfers the infrastructure financing functions of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund to a new fund managed by the DBM, with financing requests subject to council approval. It may be noted that this creates a second fund for disaster-related infrastructure repair and rehabilitation and an additional approval layer. In this regard, may we recommend that infrastructure financing remain within the NDRRMF under RA No. 10121, with insurance recoveries supplementing, and not supplanting, that fund and released through streamlined procedures, similar to Section 14 of HB No. 10763.

4.7 Section 11 (Appropriations) provides an initial and minimum fund of Php 20 billion for the new fund in its first year. It may be noted that a fixed statutory minimum reduces flexibility in budget preparation. May we recommend that initial implementation be charged against the existing appropriations of the concerned agencies and that succeeding requirements be included in the annual General Appropriations Act based on the risk assessment under the framework, without a fixed minimum amount.

memo_part.heading: On the Tax Incentive for Members of the Consortium
paragraphs: 4.8 Section 10 (Tax Incentive for Members of the Consortium) provides a five percent reduction in the corporate income tax of consortium members for the first five years. It may be noted that the reduction is not tied to the volume of public asset coverage provided, and the bill does not state whether it refers to percentage points or a share of the prevailing rate. In this regard, may we recommend the deletion of the provision, and we defer to the DOF on its revenue implications.

memo_part.heading: On the Premium Subsidies for GOCCs and LGUs
paragraphs: 4.9 Section 11 (Appropriations) further provides that premium payments for GOCCs and LGUs shall be included in the annual General Appropriations as national government subsidies. It may be noted that this creates a recurring obligation regardless of the fiscal capacity of the entities concerned. May we recommend that national assistance for LGU premiums be targeted and risk-based, with eligibility conditions such as asset registration and counterpart funding, similar to Section 9 of HB No. 10763, and that GOCCs fund their own premiums.

memo_part.heading: On the Annual Report
paragraphs: 4.10 Section 13 (Annual Report) requires a report on the progress and status of implementation. May we recommend that the required content be specified, including disaster fiscal risks, financial protection gaps, coverage of critical public assets, and claims and payout performance, similar to Section 15 of HB No. 10763, to allow assessment of whether the strategy closes the protection gap.

memo_part.heading: On the Implementing Rules and Regulations
paragraphs: 4.11 Section 15 (Implementing Rules and Regulations) requires the council to issue the implementing rules within ninety days. It may be noted that a newly created body would need to organize while also developing the framework, insurance policies and fund guidelines. May we recommend that the period be extended to 180 days, with phased implementation and consultation with LGUs and the insurance sector, similar to Sections 16 and 17 of HB No. 10763.

self_critique.objection: Build-Operate-Transfer assets return to the Government and serve the public, so leaving them out of the strategy could leave service gaps after disasters if private insurance proves inadequate.

Section 5 makes the DBM and DEPDev vice-chairs and includes the DPWH and GSIS, which gives budget, planning and implementing agencies a binding role that a DOF-BTr lead with mere coordination may not secure.
self_critique.condition: The recommendation holds only if the DOF-led arrangement formally requires DBM, DEPDev, DPWH and GSIS participation in approving the framework.

self_critique.objection: A single council with both policy and operational powers could provide clearer accountability than splitting functions among the GSIS, BTr and DOF.
A consortium of all insurers could add domestic capacity and competition that GSIS reinsurance alone may not mobilize, given the scale of public asset exposure.
self_critique.condition: The recommendation holds only if GSIS reinsurance and pooling arrangements are shown to provide enough capacity for the covered assets; otherwise a voluntary pool may be considered.

self_critique.objection: Leaving claims evaluation to a consortium led by the GSIS keeps procedures flexible and allows faster adaptation than statutory claims standards.
A dedicated fund ring-fences money for infrastructure repair so it is not crowded out by relief and response needs drawn from the NDRRMF after a disaster.
self_critique.condition: The recommendation holds only if the NDRRMF release guidelines separately track and protect the infrastructure financing layer.

self_critique.objection: Section 10 is limited to five years and requires congressional review, and an incentive may be needed to draw private insurers into public asset coverage they do not now offer.
self_critique.condition: The recommendation holds unless the DOF finds the revenue cost justified by additional coverage, in which case the incentive could be tied to public asset premiums written.

self_critique.objection: A statutory minimum guarantees resources in the first year and signals commitment, which annual appropriations cannot assure.
Universal subsidies ensure all public assets are insured, while targeting may leave poorer LGUs that fail eligibility conditions uninsured.
A detailed report list adds workload to a new body and may be better left to the implementing rules.
An independent actuarial and program review every three years, as in HB No. 10763, would test premium adequacy and coverage more rigorously than a congressional sunset review within five years.
self_critique.condition: Retention holds only if the annual report includes actuarial and claims performance information that the oversight committee can use.

self_critique.objection: A ninety-day period pushes early action on a gap the explanatory note describes as urgent.

theory_of_change.problem: Disasters damage government infrastructure and there is no multi-layered, pre-arranged financing to repair it quickly.
theory_of_change.mechanism: A council-led framework, a GSIS-led insurance consortium and a dedicated infrastructure fund provide insurance and non-insurance financing for public assets.
theory_of_change.outcome: Faster repair, reconstruction and rehabilitation of public assets and continuity of public services after disasters.
theory_of_change.weakest_assumption: That insurers will join a consortium and price public asset cover affordably, and that asset data in the NARS is complete enough to set coverage.

Check the truncated text of Section 6 beyond item (j).
Confirm whether HB No. 10763 is pending in the same Congress and committee.
